rationale: A wins because it sees that "REI won't say how much of its business is used gear" is not a nuisance to dodge; it is a real accountability angle with a reporter, a why-now, and a proof path. B is solid, but it trips over the same opening by saying "There is no data angle without the number," which is exactly backwards: the missing denominator is the story if REI wants sustainability credit. A separates operations, ownership, data, and labor cleanly; B's "Your old tent now has a trade-in price at the local REI" starts turning the same rollout into lifestyle color before the facts can carry it.
gaps_in_A: "a public retailer answering to shareholders has a hard time cheering on resale, which cannibalizes new-product margin" is a plausible business tension, but it is not in the update. Frame it as a question unless REI supplies economics or third-party retail context.

"Trade-in counters and repair benches arrive" assumes physical counters and repair benches in every store. The update says members can get repairs at any store; it does not prove on-site repair capacity.
"REI won't say" is a shade too prosecutorial. The fact set says the share of sales from used gear is not disclosed, not that REI refused a request.
gaps_in_B: "There is no data angle without the number" is the biggest miss. The non-disclosure is itself a sustainability-accountability angle if handled honestly.
"Your old tent now has a trade-in price at the local REI" invents a specific accepted item. The update says used gear, not tents, packs, zippers, or typical credit amounts.
"pilot to standard infrastructure" and "the experiment ended" overstate the program history. The update says online and select stores, not a formal pilot or experiment.

"the co-op had its best year for members" overclaims. A largest-ever dividend does not prove the best year financially or for members without the dividend amount, membership base, and prior-year comparison.
